title: Parikshit and the act of truth
hookLine: Abhimanyu's son is born without breath, and the women of the house turn to Krishna
carry: satya: a truthful life gives a promise power
tomorrow: Arjuna's son greets him with gifts. why does Arjuna want a fight?

cards: After the night raid, Ashvatthama loosed a terrible weapon he couldn't call back, and turned it on the wombs of the Pandava women. Krishna answered him then with a promise: the child Uttara is carrying will live.
Now the Pandavas are away in the mountains, fetching Marutta's gold. Uttara, Abhimanyu's young widow, goes into labor. The child is born, and he doesn't breathe.
Kunti, Draupadi, Subhadra and Uttara herself are in that room. The promise is called in.

teach.b: The grief here is not quiet. Kunti, Abhimanyu's grandmother, reminds Krishna of his words: you promised this child would live. Subhadra, Krishna's own sister and Abhimanyu's mother, pleads with him.

And Uttara speaks to the still baby in her arms, in Ganguli's telling, as if he could hear: your father died young, and now you have gone after him. Krishna goes into the birth room. He doesn't bargain or cast a weapon.

He makes a declaration of truth. He names truths about his own life: that he has never spoken a falsehood, not even in jest, that he has never turned his back in battle, that righteousness is dear to him.
By the force of those truths, he says, let this child live.
The child stirs, and breathes. This boy is Parikshit, and the dynasty that was nearly erased goes on through him. Here's the teaching.
Hindus call it satya, truth, and treat it as a real power.

teach.h: SATYAM EVA JAYATE: TRUTH ALONE WINS
teach.b: The Mundaka Upanishad says satyam eva jayate, truth alone wins; India carries those words under its national emblem. The epic shows what that means: a promise is only as strong as the life behind it.
Krishna's word could hold a child because he hadn't spent his words carelessly, even in jest. Many teachers read the scene that way. Truthfulness isn't only not lying.
It's a life whose words can be leaned on when it counts.

how: Parikshit's revival is told in the Ashvamedhika Parva, and Hindu tradition remembers Parikshit as the king to whom, in the Bhagavata Purana, the sage Shuka later recites that text.

games.q: a friend says a promise is just words; what matters is whether you still feel like keeping it. by Parikshit's story, what fits?
o: satya gives words weight: Krishna's truthful life is why his promise could save a child.
right: promises are only words, and feelings matter more.
promises only count when they're made to a god.
games.why: Krishna saved the child with a declaration of truth, naming the truths of his life. satyam eva jayate: truth alone wins.

practice: Many Hindus begin a puja with a sankalpa, a solemn intention spoken aloud, sometimes with a little water held in the right palm.

Cup your right hand, and name, plainly, one promise you're still keeping, to a child, a friend, a parent, yourself. Then say one true sentence about how you try to live, one you could say out loud and mean, and open your hand.
If you pray, offer that sentence in your prayer; if you don't, just let it be said.

wordCard.voice: Ashvamedhika. The book where a child born without breath lives, by a promise kept and a truth spoken aloud.
